source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. XI (Montreuil)

1.title: De perfectione evangelicæ legis
1.title_en: On the perfection of the Gospel law
1.note: A general introduction to the commentary on Luke: Denis expounds no verse of the Gospel here (the prologue, 1:1–4, begins in Art. II), so the article is placed at the head of chapter 1.

paras.t: Ecce Deus excelsus in fortitudine sua, et nullus ei similis in legislatoribus. Job xxxvi, 22. Quemadmodum in Prima Secundæ Thomas ostendit, lex est regula atque mensura actuum, per quam quis ad agendum vel non agendum bene se habet sive inducitur. Legis enim est, actus hominum regulare debito ordine secundum exigentiam finis a legislatore intenti.
paras.en: [[Job 36:22|Behold, God is high in his strength, and none is like him among the lawgivers.|Ecce Deus excelsus in fortitudine sua, et nullus ei similis in legislatoribus]] As Thomas shows in the Prima Secundæ [the first part of the second part of his *Summa theologiae*], law is a rule and measure of acts, by which one is well disposed, or led, to act or not to act. For it belongs to law to regulate the acts of men in due order, according to what is required by the end intended by the lawgiver.

paras.t: Multiplex autem lex ponitur, videlicet: lex æterna, quæ est dictamen et ratio divinæ sapientiæ, in quantum est directiva actionum ac motuum omnium creaturarum. De qua lege Deo Sapiens ait: Quum sis justus, juste omnia disponis; virtus enim tua justitiæ initium est. Hæc itaque lex realiter idem est quod summa et increata Sapientia, attingens a fine usque ad finem fortiter, et disponens cuncta suaviter: quæ lex, secundum Anselmum in libro de Veritate, omnis rectitudinis et virtutis, omnis veritatis ac legis origo est, et fontale atque causale principium. — Alia est ergo lex naturalis, quæ est participatio legis æternæ, naturis rerum creatarum naturaliter indita, per quam quælibet tendit in proprium finem sibi a divina sapientia præstitutum, et operatur proprias actiones. Porro lex ista naturalis in homine est dictamen seu ordinatio vel censura practicæ rationis, per quam homo ad aliquid agendum vel omittendum inducitur. Istaque lex sufficeret homini, si homo non ordinaretur nisi ad naturalem felicitatem ac finem; sed quia ad supernaturalem beatitudinem (quæ est visio Dei per speciem, seu facie ad faciem, secundum Apostolum) creatus et ordinatus est, ideo supernaturali indiget lege, quæ dicitur lex divina, per quam de vera ac supernaturali beatitudine instruatur, atque de præceptis et actibus perveniendi ad illam illuminetur. Quæ lex est mensura ac regula actuum humanorum in ordine ad felicitatem supernaturalem æternam. Siquidem per hanc legem ratio cognoscit et dictat quid de Deo sentiendum, quomodo ei obsequendum, ad quem finem sit omne nostrum exercitium referendum. De qua ait Psalmista: Lex Domini immaculata, convertens animas.
paras.en: Now law is spoken of in several ways. There is the eternal law, which is the dictate and reason of the divine wisdom, inasmuch as it directs the actions and movements of all creatures. Of this law the Wise man says to God: [[Wis 12:15|thou art just, thou orderest all things justly|Quum sis justus, juste omnia disponis]]; for [[Wis 12:16|thy power is the beginning of justice|virtus enim tua justitiæ initium est]]. This law, then, is in reality the same as the supreme and uncreated Wisdom, reaching from end to end mightily and ordering all things sweetly[[Wis 8:1||]]; and this law, according to Anselm in his book *On Truth*, is the origin of all rightness and virtue, of all truth and law, their fountain and causal principle. — Next, then, there is the natural law, which is a participation of the eternal law, implanted by nature in the natures of created things, by which each thing tends to its own end, appointed for it by the divine wisdom, and performs its proper actions. In man this natural law is the dictate, ordering or judgment of the practical reason, by which man is led to do or to leave undone some thing. And this law would suffice for man if he were ordered only to a natural happiness and end; but because he has been created and ordered to a supernatural beatitude (which is the vision of God by sight, or face to face, according to the Apostle[[1 Cor 13:12||]][[2 Cor 3:18||]]), he needs a supernatural law, which is called the divine law, by which he may be instructed about true and supernatural beatitude, and enlightened about the precepts and acts by which it is reached. This law is the measure and rule of human acts in their ordering to eternal, supernatural happiness. For by this law reason knows and dictates what is to be believed of God, how he is to be served, and to what end all our activity is to be referred. Of it the Psalmist says: [[Ps 18:8|The law of the Lord is unspotted, converting souls|Lex Domini immaculata, convertens animas]].

paras.t: Insuper, præter legem æternam et naturalem ac divinam, ponitur lex humana, quæ est quoddam rationis dictamen, quo diriguntur actus humani in ordine ad finem boni communis in vita præsenti ad convivendum pacifice: quæ lex ex naturali lege progreditur, estque determinatio et explicatio ejus circa particularia hominum opera. Quemadmodum enim ratio speculativa ex primis ac indemonstrabilibus principiis elicit varias diversarum scientiarum conclusiones: sic ratio practica ex primis principiis operativis, seu agendorum, quæ ad naturalem pertinent legem, procedit ad particulariora, inquirendo et discutiendo quid in certis negotiis sit agendum; et hujusmodi particulares dispositiones per rationem inventæ, dicuntur leges humanæ, observatis aliis conditionibus quæ ad legem concurrere debent. Lex enim concernit bonum commune. Dicit quoque Isidorus, quod lex humana, quantum possibile est, debet esse honesta, ut religioni conveniat; justa, ut secundum rationem procedat; possibilis, ut a subditis portari valeat et impleri. Erit demum secundum consuetudinem patriæ, et loco ac tempori debet congruere.
paras.en: Besides the eternal, the natural and the divine law, there is also human law, which is a certain dictate of reason by which human acts are directed to the end of the common good in the present life, so that men may live together in peace. This law proceeds from the natural law, and is its determination and application to the particular works of men. For as the speculative reason draws from first and indemonstrable principles the various conclusions of the different sciences, so the practical reason proceeds from the first principles of action, or of things to be done, which belong to the natural law, to more particular things, inquiring and discussing what is to be done in given affairs; and such particular dispositions, found out by reason, are called human laws, provided the other conditions that must go into a law are observed. For law concerns the common good. Isidore also says that human law, as far as possible, ought to be honest, so as to accord with religion; just, so as to proceed according to reason; possible, so that subjects may be able to bear it and fulfil it. It will be, finally, in keeping with the custom of the country, and ought to suit the place and the time.

paras.t: Denique lex divina dividitur in legem veterem seu Mosaicam, et novam seu evangelicam. Quæ divisio non est per diversas seu oppositas species, quum utriusque sit unus finis, scilicet Christus, seu Deo conjungi ac frui; in utraque etiam principalia præcepta, puta moralia, sunt eadem: sed est sicut dividitur aliquid per perfectum et imperfectum, quæ tamen unius sunt speciei, ut homo per virum et puerum.
paras.en: Lastly, the divine law is divided into the old or Mosaic law and the new or Gospel law. This division is not into different or opposed species, since both have one end, namely Christ[[Rom 10:4||]], that is, to be joined to God and to enjoy him; in both, too, the chief precepts, that is, the moral ones, are the same. It is rather as a thing is divided into perfect and imperfect, which are nevertheless of one species, as man is divided into grown man and boy.

paras.t: Nunc ergo ostendenda est legis evangelicæ super omnem aliam legem creatam excellentia atque perfectio. Porro, quod omnem legem humanam excedat, certum et clarum est, et infra probabitur. Quod vero legem Moysis perfectione dignitateque superet, primo ostenditur ex parte legislatoris. Vetus enim lex a Deo data est, non immediate, sed mediate, imo per gradum duplicem ministrorum, puta per angelum et per Moysen. Deo namque jubente ac destinante, locutus est angelus Moysi, jubenteque angelo ex parte Dei, Moyses legem ab angelo immediate acceptam proposuit populo. Imo non unius dumtaxat ministerio angeli, sed plurium angelorum, data est vetus lex, juxta illud Apostoli: Lex propter transgressores posita est, ordinata per angelos in manu mediatoris. Unde in Actibus Stephanus exprobrans ingratis Judæis: Accepistis legem in dispositione angelorum, et non custodistis. Evangelica vero lex a vero Deo, videlicet Jesu Christo Unigenito Patris æterni (de quo Christo in sua Canonica scribit Joannes: Hic est verus Deus et vita æterna) immediate collata est.
paras.en: Now, then, the excellence and perfection of the Gospel law above every other created law must be shown. That it surpasses every human law is certain and clear, and will be proved below. That it surpasses the law of Moses in perfection and dignity is shown, first, on the part of the lawgiver. For the old law was given by God not immediately but mediately, indeed through a double rank of ministers, namely through an angel and through Moses. At God's command and appointment the angel spoke to Moses[[Ex 19:3||]], and at the angel's command, on God's behalf, Moses set before the people the law he had received immediately from the angel. Indeed, the old law was given by the ministry not of one angel only but of many, according to the Apostle's words: The law [[Gal 3:19|was set because of transgressions|propter transgressores posita est]] [Denis's text reads *transgressores*, "transgressors", where the Vulgate has *transgressiones*], [[Gal 3:19|being ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator|ordinata per angelos in manu mediatoris]]. Hence in the Acts Stephen, reproaching the ungrateful Jews, says: You [[Acts 7:53|have received the law by the disposition of angels and have not kept it|Accepistis legem in dispositione angelorum, et non custodistis]]. But the Gospel law was bestowed immediately by the true God, that is, by Jesus Christ, the Only-begotten of the eternal Father (of which Christ John writes in his canonical Epistle: [[1 John 5:20|This is the true God and life eternal|Hic est verus Deus et vita æterna]]).

paras.t: Secundo ostenditur idem, quia vetus lex comparatur ad novam sicut imperfectum ad perfectum, sicut medium ad finem, sicut dispositio ad formam seu habitum; imo lex evangelica se habet ad veterem legem sicut meridies ad auroram, lumen ad umbram, veritas ad figuram, domina ad ancillam. Quum enim finis legis divinæ, videlicet veteris ac novæ, sit ad veram felicitatem perducere seu Deo uniri ac frui, illa lex divina vocatur perfecta, quæ ea includit per quæ beatitudo acquiritur, ad quam sine gratia gratum faciente nemo perducitur. Vetus autem lex gratiam non continuit, sed promisit. Evangelica vero lex gratiam includit et confert, quoniam sacramenta ejus gratiam non solum figurant, seu signant, sed etiam conferunt, et efficiunt quod designant. Ideo dicit Apostolus: Nihil ad perfectum adduxit lex, introductio vero melioris spei, per quam approximamus ad Deum; rursus: Lex pædagogus noster fuit in Christo Jesu; itemque: Si data esset lex quæ posset vivificare, vere ex lege esset justitia; sed conclusit Scriptura omnia sub peccato. Hujus autem ratio assignatur, quoniam sacramenta veteris legis gratiam non continebant nec conferebant; sed ipsa lex dispositiva fuit ad evangelicam legem, eam præfigurando, Christum prænuntiando, idololatriam reprobando, ideo Christi lege promulgata cessavit. Propter quod dicit Apostolus: Priusquam veniret fides, sub lege custodiebamur, conclusi in eam fidem quæ revelanda erat; ubi autem venit fides, jam non sumus sub pædagogo. Similiter loquitur ad Hebræos: Reprobatio quidem fit præcedentis mandati propter infirmitatem et inutilitatem.
paras.en: Secondly, the same is shown because the old law is compared to the new as the imperfect to the perfect, as the means to the end, as a disposition to the form or habit; indeed, the Gospel law stands to the old law as midday to the dawn, light to shadow, truth to the figure, the mistress to the handmaid. For since the end of the divine law, both old and new, is to lead to true happiness, that is, to be united to God and to enjoy him, that divine law is called perfect which contains the things by which beatitude is gained; and to beatitude no one is brought without sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes a man pleasing to God]. But the old law did not contain grace; it promised it. The Gospel law contains and confers grace, since its sacraments not only figure or signify grace but also confer it, and effect what they signify. Therefore the Apostle says: [[Heb 7:19|the law brought nothing to perfection: but a bringing in of a better hope, by which we draw nigh to God|Nihil ad perfectum adduxit lex, introductio vero melioris spei, per quam approximamus ad Deum]]; and again: [[Gal 3:24|the law was our pedagogue in Christ|Lex pædagogus noster fuit in Christo]] Jesus [the *pædagogus* was the slave who led a boy to school and kept him in order until he came of age]; and also: [[Gal 3:21|if there had been a law given which could give life, verily justice should have been by the law|Si data esset lex quæ posset vivificare, vere ex lege esset justitia]]; [[Gal 3:22|But the scripture hath concluded all under sin|sed conclusit Scriptura omnia sub peccato]]. The reason given for this is that the sacraments of the old law did not contain or confer grace; but the law itself was a preparation for the Gospel law, prefiguring it, foretelling Christ, condemning idolatry; and so, once the law of Christ was promulgated, it ceased. That is why the Apostle says: [[Gal 3:23|before the faith came, we were kept under the law shut up, unto that faith which was to be revealed|Priusquam veniret fides, sub lege custodiebamur, conclusi in eam fidem quæ revelanda erat]]; [[Gal 3:25|But after the faith is come, we are no longer under a pedagogue|ubi autem venit fides, jam non sumus sub pædagogo]]. In the same way he speaks to the Hebrews: [[Heb 7:18|There is indeed a setting aside of the former commandment, because of the weakness and unprofitableness thereof|Reprobatio quidem fit præcedentis mandati propter infirmitatem et inutilitatem]].

paras.t: Tertio, idem probatur, quia lex evangelica bona cœlestia et futura in patria manifeste prænuntiat, figurat, promittit, atque ad ea immediate introducit. Horum autem bonorum lex vetus non habuit significationem expressam et propinquam, sed obscuram atque remotam, prout scriptum est: Umbram habens lex futurorum bonorum, non ipsam imaginem rerum. Hinc, juxta divum Dionysium, status evangelicæ legis medius est inter statum Synagogæ seu veteris legis, ac patriæ: ita quod sacramenta et cærimonialia novæ legis habent imaginem perfectam et evidentem similitudinem bonorum cœlestium, quorum umbram gerebant sacramenta ac cærimonialia veteris Testamenti, quia in veteri lege bona illa ventura promittebantur, et figurabantur sub velamine et confuse. Denique dicitur lex evangelica gratiam continere et dare, per inclusionem sacramentorum suorum, hoc est, in quantum includit Christi sacramenta, quæ sunt spiritualiter medicinalia vasa. Et quoniam lex vetus talia sacramenta gratiæ contentiva non habuit, ideo propria virtute non justificavit, sed fide et gratia Christi tunc venturi, per cujus fidem opera hominum sub lege positorum meritoria erant. Hinc ab Apostolo dicitur lex illa subintrasse, ut abundaret delictum, et quod per eam peccatum revixit; itemque, quod fuit administratio mortis, non utique causaliter et directe, sed occasionaliter et consecutive, et quoniam gratiam non præstabat; rursusque, quia peccatum post legislationem gravius fuit quam ante, et quoniam talis est nostra perversitas, quod nitimur in vetitum, et ea quæ nobis prohibentur, magis optamus.
paras.en: Thirdly, the same is proved because the Gospel law openly foretells, figures and promises the heavenly goods to come in our true country, and leads straight into them. Of these goods the old law had no express and near signification, but only an obscure and remote one, as it is written: [[Heb 10:1|the law, having a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things|Umbram habens lex futurorum bonorum, non ipsam imaginem rerum]]. Hence, according to the divine Dionysius, the state of the Gospel law is midway between the state of the Synagogue, or of the old law, and that of our heavenly country: so that the sacraments and ceremonies of the new law have a perfect image and evident likeness of the heavenly goods, of which the sacraments and ceremonies of the Old Testament bore the shadow; for in the old law those goods to come were promised and figured under a veil and confusedly. Further, the Gospel law is said to contain and give grace by its inclusion of its sacraments, that is, inasmuch as it includes the sacraments of Christ, which are vessels of spiritual medicine. And since the old law had no such sacraments containing grace, it did not justify by its own power, but by faith in Christ, then still to come, and by his grace; through faith in him the works of men placed under the law were meritorious. Hence the Apostle says that this law [[Rom 5:20|entered in that sin might abound|subintrasse, ut abundaret delictum]], and that through it [[Rom 7:9|sin revived|peccatum revixit]]; and also that it was [[2 Cor 3:7|the ministration of death|administratio mortis]] [the margin reference is read as II Cor. i, 4; the words are those of 2 Cor 3:7]: not, indeed, as its cause and directly, but as its occasion and consequently, and because it did not give grace; and again, because sin was graver after the giving of the law than before it, and because such is our perversity that we strive after what is forbidden, and long the more for the things that are forbidden us.

paras.t: Quarto declaratur id ipsum, videlicet excellentia et perfectio legis evangelicæ super omnem aliam legem divinam atque humanam, quoniam proprietates et actus legis eminentius ei conveniunt quam alicui alteri legi. — Quum enim legis officium sit homines facere virtuosos, et primo oporteat declinare a malo: ideo primo ad legem pertinet vitia exstirpare per comminationem seu inflictionem pœnarum, seu alio modo: quod propter vitiosos, protervos, et ad mala proclives, potissimum necessarium est; et quantum ad hoc dicit Apostolus: Justo non est lex posita, sed injustis, et non subditis, impiis et sceleratis. Hoc autem lex humana perfecte non efficit: nam quia communitati proponitur, in qua plures sunt imperfecti, vitiosi, ad malaque proni, quædam mala permittit ne deteriora contingant, videlicet meretrices et usurarios, quæ tamen divino relinquit judicio punienda, secundum quod asserit Augustinus: Lex quæ regendis civitatibus datur, multa concedit ac impunita relinquit, quæ per divinam providentiam vindicantur. Lex quoque Mosaica divinitus lata, quia populo rudi ad maxima mala proclivi dabatur, quædam mala permisit, ut dare libellum repudii et ad usuram extraneis accommodare, ut patet in Deuteronomio, ne majora mala incurrerentur, videlicet ne Judæi uxores suas occiderent, neque fratribus suis ad usuram concederent. Hinc Christus ait Judæis: Ad duritiam cordis vestri, Moyses permisit vobis dare libellum repudii. Lex autem evangelica tanquam perfecta, nullum prorsus malum permittit, sed omne peccatum excludit, et puniendum testatur, imo de omni verbo otioso rationem Deo reddendam fatetur.
paras.en: Fourthly, the same thing is made clear, namely the excellence and perfection of the Gospel law above every other law, divine and human, because the properties and acts of law belong to it more eminently than to any other law. — For since the office of law is to make men virtuous, and one must first decline from evil[[Ps 36:27||]], it belongs to law, first, to root out vices by threatening or inflicting punishments, or in some other way; and this is most of all necessary because of the vicious, the froward and those prone to evil. As to this the Apostle says: [[1 Tim 1:9|the law is not made for the just man but for the unjust and disobedient, for the ungodly|Justo non est lex posita, sed injustis, et non subditis, impiis]], and [[1 Tim 1:9|for the wicked|sceleratis]]. Human law does not do this perfectly: for since it is set before a community in which many are imperfect, vicious and prone to evil, it permits certain evils lest worse should happen, for instance harlots and usurers; these, however, it leaves to the judgment of God for punishment, as Augustine asserts: The law that is given for the governing of cities grants many things and leaves them unpunished, which are avenged by divine providence. The Mosaic law too, though given by God, because it was given to a rude people very prone to the greatest evils, permitted certain evils, such as giving a bill of divorce[[Deut 24:1||]] and lending at usury to strangers[[Deut 23:19||]], as is plain in Deuteronomy, lest greater evils be incurred, namely lest the Jews kill their wives, or lend at usury to their brethren. Hence Christ says to the Jews: [[Matt 19:8|Moses by reason of the hardness of your heart permitted you|Ad duritiam cordis vestri, Moyses permisit vobis]] [[Matt 19:7|to give a bill of divorce|dare libellum repudii]]. But the Gospel law, being perfect, permits no evil whatever, but excludes all sin and declares that it is to be punished; indeed, it professes that an account must be rendered to God for every idle word[[Matt 12:36||]].

paras.t: — Secundo, ad legem pertinet virtutes inducere, seu mores componere: quod lex humana non facit perfecte. Homo enim interiora aliorum non intuetur, idcirco de secretis cordium judicare non valet: ideo lex humana non nisi exteriores actus habet ordinare et judicare. Interiores vero affectus et cogitatus reformare et rectificare, ad legem spectat divinam; sed et lex Mosaica non facit hoc plene. Propter quod dicunt doctores, quod cohibet manum seu opus, non animum: quod intelligendum non est, quasi voluntatem malam nequaquam prohibeat, vel in cogitationibus vitium non consistat, quum Moyses dicat in Exodo, Non concupisces uxorem proximi tui, non bovem, non ancillam, non agrum, nec omnia quæ illius sunt; sed hoc ideo dicitur, quia lex Moysis non tam plene et evidenter prohibet inordinatum affectum et cogitatum, nec tantum versatur circa interiorem reformationem sicut lex nova. Verumtamen in multis ordinavit interiores affectus, nec solam respicit inordinatam affectionem in vitiis avaritiæ atque luxuriæ, ut aliqui dicunt, sed et in aliis multis. Unde in Levitico legitur: Ne oderis fratrem tuum in corde tuo, nec memor eris injuriæ civium tuorum. Et in Deuteronomio habetur: Custodi te ipsum et animam tuam sollicite, ne obliviscaris verborum Domini Dei tui, et ne excidant de corde tuo cunctis diebus vitæ tuæ. Rursus in Deuteronomio præcipitur: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo et ex tota anima tua, et ex tota fortitudine tua. Nihilominus, si tota lex Moysis percurratur, patebit quod comparative loquendo, paucissima de interiorum directione et ordinatione loquatur, sed circa exteriora permaxime occupetur. Quod autem modicum est quasi pro nihilo computatur, sicque dici potuit, quod lex vetus manum non animum cohibebat.
paras.en: — Secondly, it belongs to law to bring in the virtues, or to set behaviour in order; and human law does not do this perfectly. For man does not see into the inward parts of others, and so cannot judge the secrets of hearts; therefore human law can only order and judge outward acts. To reform and set right the inward affections and thoughts belongs to the divine law; but the Mosaic law, too, does not do this fully. That is why the doctors say that it restrains the hand, or the deed, but not the mind. This is not to be understood as if it in no way forbade an evil will, or as if vice did not lie in the thoughts, since Moses says in Exodus[[Ex 20:17||]]: [[Deut 5:21|Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife|Non concupisces uxorem proximi tui]], not his ox, nor his handmaid, nor his field, [[Deut 5:21|nor any thing that is his|nec omnia quæ illius sunt]] [Denis names Exodus, but his wording is nearer that of Deuteronomy 5:21, which the margin also gives]. It is said rather because the law of Moses does not forbid inordinate affection and thought so fully and plainly as the new law, nor is it so much concerned with inward reform. Yet in many things it did order the inward affections; and it does not regard only inordinate affection in the vices of avarice and lust, as some say, but in many others too. Hence we read in Leviticus: [[Lev 19:17|Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart|Ne oderis fratrem tuum in corde tuo]], [[Lev 19:18|nor be mindful of the injury of thy citizens|nec memor eris injuriæ civium tuorum]]. And in Deuteronomy we have: [[Deut 4:9|Keep thyself|Custodi te ipsum]], and [[Deut 4:9|thy soul carefully|animam tuam sollicite]]; [[Deut 4:9|Forget not the words|ne obliviscaris verborum]] of the Lord thy God, [[Deut 4:9|and let them not go out of thy heart all the days of thy life|et ne excidant de corde tuo cunctis diebus vitæ tuæ]]. Again, it is commanded in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 6:5|Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, and with thy whole soul, and with thy whole strength.|Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo et ex tota anima tua, et ex tota fortitudine tua]] Nevertheless, if the whole law of Moses be gone through, it will be clear that, comparatively speaking, it says very little about the direction and ordering of inward things, and is taken up very largely with outward ones. And what is little is reckoned as nothing; and so it could be said that the old law restrained the hand and not the mind.

paras.t: — Præterea, quoniam virtus ad beatitudinem ordinatur, ideo ad legem tertio pertinet, ad felicitatem perducere. Vera autem hominis beatitudo est supernaturalis: ad quam lex humana seu naturalis nequit perducere, sed supernaturalis dumtaxat. Rursus, ad felicitatem supernaturalem non pertingitur, nisi per gratiam gratificantem, quam (ut patuit) lex Moysis non continebat, nec conferebat, idcirco nec ipsa ad felicitatem sua virtute perduxit: quod lex Christi per sua efficit sacramenta, quæ de latere Christi in cruce dormientis fluxerunt, efficaciamque sortita sunt, ita quod per ea virtus et meritum passionis Christi hominibus applicatur. Ideo in evangelio Joannis inducitur: Lex per Moysen data est, gratia et veritas per Jesum Christum facta est.
paras.en: — Further, since virtue is ordered to beatitude, it belongs to law, thirdly, to lead to happiness. But man's true beatitude is supernatural, and to it human or natural law cannot lead, but only supernatural law. Again, supernatural happiness is not reached except through sanctifying grace, which (as has been shown) the law of Moses did not contain or confer; and so neither did it lead to happiness by its own power. This the law of Christ does by its sacraments, which flowed from the side of Christ as he slept on the cross and drew their efficacy from it, so that through them the power and merit of Christ's passion are applied to men. Therefore it is set down in the Gospel of John: [[John 1:17|the law was given by Moses: grace and truth came by Jesus Christ|Lex per Moysen data est, gratia et veritas per Jesum Christum facta est]].

paras.t: — Insuper, quoniam lex pro communi datur utilitate, quarto spectat ad eam, ut omnibus promulgetur, et clare ac intelligibiliter proponatur, quia in communitate major pars grossa est, nec subtilia, difficilia, profundaque penetrat. Lex autem evangelica compendiosissime ac succincte datur atque proponitur. Mosaica vero lex multis velaminibus tegitur, et figuris involvitur; in qua etiam eadem sæpius repetuntur, et difficillimum fuit singula ejus præcepta memoriter continere, efficaciterque implere. Propter quod Petrus apostolus ait in Actibus de onere legis, Quod neque nos neque patres nostri portare potuimus.
paras.en: — Moreover, since law is given for the common good, it belongs to it, fourthly, to be promulgated to all and set forth clearly and intelligibly, because in a community the greater part is unlearned and does not penetrate subtle, difficult and deep things. Now the Gospel law is given and set forth most compendiously and briefly. But the Mosaic law is covered with many veils[[2 Cor 3:14||]] and wrapped in figures; in it, too, the same things are often repeated, and it was most difficult to hold each of its precepts in memory and to fulfil them effectively. That is why the apostle Peter says in the Acts, of the burden of the law: [[Acts 15:10|which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?|Quod neque nos neque patres nostri portare potuimus]].

paras.t: Adhuc autem evangelicæ legis eminentia constat ex hoc, quod vetus lex aperte atque communiter non promisit nisi bona terrena, de cœlesti præmio evidenter non loquens. Evangelica vero lex, cœlestia bona, spiritualem opulentiam, æternam ac deiformem beatitudinem apertissime et copiosissime pollicetur. Unde in principio prædicationis evangelicæ dicitur: Pœnitentiam agite, appropinquabit enim regnum cœlorum. — Postremo, lex Christi ad observantiam sui inducit amore boni; lex autem Moysis, timore pœnarum: ideo, secundum Augustinum, brevis differentia legis et Evangelii est amor et timor. Unde Apostolus: Non dedit nobis Deus spiritum timoris, sed virtutis et dilectionis et sobrietatis.
paras.en: The eminence of the Gospel law is further established by this: that the old law openly and generally promised nothing but earthly goods, and did not speak plainly of the heavenly reward; whereas the Gospel law most openly and most abundantly promises heavenly goods, spiritual riches, an eternal and godlike beatitude. Hence at the very beginning of the Gospel preaching it is said: [[Matt 3:2|Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand|Pœnitentiam agite, appropinquabit enim regnum cœlorum]][[Matt 4:17||]]. — Lastly, the law of Christ leads men to keep it by love of the good, but the law of Moses by fear of punishment; therefore, according to Augustine, the difference between the Law and the Gospel, in brief, is love and fear. Hence the Apostle: [[2 Tim 1:7|God hath not given us the spirit of fear: but of power and of love and of sobriety|Non dedit nobis Deus spiritum timoris, sed virtutis et dilectionis et sobrietatis]].

paras.t: Itaque de legislatore nostro unico Dei Filio vere accipitur, quod in principio hujus articuli dictum est: Ecce Deus excelsus in fortitudine sua, et nullus ei similis in legislatoribus. De quo Isaias ait: Dominus judex noster, Dominus legifer noster, Dominus rex noster, ipse veniet et salvabit nos. Interea, quo major est dignitas legiferi hujus, et quo major est caritas, beneficentia et dignatio ejus ad nos, in hoc quod pro nostra salute, in propria persona descendit ad nos, et proprio ore legem nobis deprompsit; quo etiam major est excellentia atque perfectio legis istius: eo gravior est nostra ingratitudo, perversitas et impietas, si legislatori huic inobedientes fuerimus. Propter quod dicit Apostolus: Irritam quis faciens legem Moysis, sine ulla contradictione, duobus vel tribus testibus moritur: quanto magis putatis deteriora mereri supplicia, qui Filium Dei conculcaverit, et sanguinem testamenti pollutum duxerit, et Spiritui gratiæ contumeliam fecerit? Hinc ergo quo noster legifer exstat sublimior, et quo benignius se habuit circa nos, quo item præclariorem nobis contulit legem, eo diligentiores, ferventiores, efficacioresque simus in observatione suæ legis condigna, cum metu et reverentia servientes: scientes, quia cui plus datum est, plus requiretur ab eo; et servus sciens voluntatem domini sui nec faciens, plagis vapulabit multis.
paras.en: Thus what was said at the beginning of this article is truly understood of our lawgiver, the only Son of God: [[Job 36:22|Behold, God is high in his strength, and none is like him among the lawgivers.|Ecce Deus excelsus in fortitudine sua, et nullus ei similis in legislatoribus]] Of him Isaias says: [[Is 33:22|the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king|Dominus judex noster, Dominus legifer noster, Dominus rex noster]]: he will come and [[Is 33:22|save us|salvabit nos]]. Meanwhile, the greater the dignity of this lawgiver, and the greater his charity, kindness and condescension towards us, in that for our salvation he came down to us in his own person and with his own mouth delivered the law to us, and the greater the excellence and perfection of this law, so much the graver is our ingratitude, perversity and impiety if we are disobedient to this lawgiver. That is why the Apostle says: [[Heb 10:28|A man making void the law of Moses dieth|Irritam quis faciens legem Moysis]] without any gainsaying [Denis's text reads *sine ulla contradictione*; the Vulgate has *miseratione*, "without any mercy"] [[Heb 10:28|under two or three witnesses|duobus vel tribus testibus moritur]]: [[Heb 10:29|How much more, do you think he deserveth worse punishments, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God and hath esteemed the blood of the testament unclean|quanto magis putatis deteriora mereri supplicia, qui Filium Dei conculcaverit, et sanguinem testamenti pollutum duxerit]], [[Heb 10:29|and hath offered an affront to the Spirit of grace?|et Spiritui gratiæ contumeliam fecerit?]] Hence, then, the more exalted our lawgiver is, and the more kindly he has dealt with us, and the more excellent the law he has given us, the more diligent, fervent and effective let us be in the worthy keeping of his law, serving with fear and reverence[[Phil 2:12||]] [the margin gives Phil. ii, 12, "with fear and trembling"; Denis's words are nearer Heb 12:28, "let us serve, pleasing God, with fear and reverence"]: knowing that [[Luke 12:48|unto whomsoever much is given, of him much shall be required|cui plus datum est, plus requiretur ab eo]]; and that [[Luke 12:47|that servant, who knew the will of his lord|servus sciens voluntatem domini sui]] and doing it not [[Luke 12:47|shall be beaten with many stripes|plagis vapulabit multis]].
